title: Clash Time, Baby!
author: Wess Trabelsi
summary: Wess Trabelsi uses Dan Meyer's new grading policy as the occasion to air a long-standing objection to prominent AI skeptics: they critique vendor promises well but rarely tell teachers what to do tomorrow morning. He recalls that Meyer once dismissed the idea of teachers reviewing student chatbot conversations as science fiction, a jab aimed in part at Mike Kentz and the so-called grade-the-chats camp. Meyer's October 2026 policy now puts 80 percent of the grade on in-class exams without AI and 20 percent on completion-graded homework where students may use AI freely, while inviting them to share their prompts for feedback. Trabelsi reads this as a tactical retreat that concedes the premise of his side: students will use AI regardless, and teachers need to stop policing authorship. He remains unsure the policy scales to young or far-behind students, and he sees an adversarial edge in it. He closes by asking skeptics like Meyer, Ben Riley, and Dylan Kane to put their ingenuity into constructive classroom designs, such as messy real-world problems that make students decide what information matters.
points: Trabelsi argues that critiquing edtech hype is necessary but insufficient, because teachers still face students who already use chatbots and need workable practice.

Meyer's policy of 80 percent in-class exams and 20 percent completion-graded homework treats AI-assisted homework as practice rather than evidence, which removes the teacher from the role of authorship detective.

Inviting students to submit their prompts for feedback is, in Trabelsi's view, the same insight behind grade-the-chats: a student's conversation with a chatbot reveals what they understand and where they are confused.
He doubts that final-exam stakes will motivate struggling students and admits he has no better answer, which keeps the piece honest rather than triumphant.
His hopeful alternative is to use AI to expand the kinds of real, under- or over-specified problems students can tackle, if someone can solve the problem of keeping students persistent.
quotes: But the “grade the chats” guys were at least trying to address a problem that wasn’t going to disappear because we disapproved of it.
His proposed response is interesting. Exams, taken in class without AI, would count for 80% of the grade. Homework would count for 20%, graded on completion alone.

When you read how a student talks to a chatbot, you can get an indication of what’s in their head: what they understand, what they’re confused about, what they’re trying to do. That’s useful information for a teacher.

This is the frustration I have when I read Dan, Ben Riley, or Dylan Kane. I often agree with their criticisms, but I want to hear what they think teachers should try while students keep using these tools.
But he’s trying to do something I think is essential: getting teachers out of the business of policing how, or how much, students use AI.
There’s an adversarial edge to the policy, even though Dan presents it as a way to repair the relationship between teachers and students.
You can get good at decoding the textbook without getting very good at solving problems.
